body: Please do not use LLMs to write issue descriptions, assuming as this reads like the original description of your PR, please remove unnecessary text as this is far too verbose
Shortened and reused most of the PR description.

> Constructing a `RandomNumberGenerator` completes in well under a microsecond on modern hardware, so consecutive `RandomNumberGenerator.new()` calls in the same frame routinely read the same timestamp, get the same seed, and emit byte-identical streams.

This doesn't match what you said in the PR description:
> Approximately 200 to 800 ns per `randomize()` call on top of the existing 1 to 5 us construction. No measurable frame-time impact.

What does the 1 to 5 us mean in that case?

I don't think this test setup is appropriate, it doesn't actually test the seed overlap, it tests a very specific case of randomness "error", in consecutive random generated samples from two different seeds are equal, which for 5 samples isn't impossible

If instead you do this:
```gdscript
var rolls: PackedInt64Array = []
for t in TRIALS:
	var rng := RandomNumberGenerator.new()
	rolls.push_back(rng.seed)
var ties := 0
for t in range(1, TRIALS):
	if rolls[t] == rolls[t - 1]: ties += 1
print("ties: %d" % ties)
```

You find that there are no overlaps at all in the actual seeds, even though the rolls test shows supposed errors (even added a version that tests for both, which got 2 ties for the roll values, but not for the actual seeds, showing this fact)

Can you provide some test case that actually shows seeds overlapping?

Edit: Correction, in an exported project it does show both overlapping, so with a properly formatted test it does occur

The problem itself isn't necessarily guaranteed from that though, it isn't necessarily a valid case

While I can confirm the specific scenario with a faster template I don't see that this is a remotely common use case, generating a large number of RNGs in a without some custom seeding mechanism seems very very niche and potentially a code smell, and I think it would be better to document that creating RNGs very rapidly can cause the seeds to overlap, and suggest using other means to improve this

Two things.

On the "1 to 5 us" line in the PR description, that was an initial estimate I jotted down before benchmarking. Once I ran the 100M test on a fresh Windows desktop and saw per-iteration of 428 ns end to end, I should have gone back and corrected it but didn't. Real per-iteration cost of `RandomNumberGenerator.new()` plus reading `seed` is around 300 to 400 ns on both an M-series Mac and a fast Windows desktop in release headless builds. The bug triggers when per-iteration time falls under one microsecond, which is the entropy resolution of the seed formula. I'll fix that line in the description.

On the seed overlap test, you're right that the proper test should look at `rng.seed` directly rather than infer from output. I just ran your exact snippet (extended to 1M trials and tracking distinct seeds too) on two machines:

```gdscript
const TRIALS := 1_000_000

func _ready() -> void:
    var t0 := Time.get_ticks_usec()
    var seeds := PackedInt64Array(); seeds.resize(TRIALS)
    for t in TRIALS:
        var rng := RandomNumberGenerator.new()
        seeds[t] = rng.seed
    var elapsed_us := Time.get_ticks_usec() - t0
    var ties := 0
    for t in range(1, TRIALS):
        if seeds[t] == seeds[t - 1]: ties += 1
    var distinct := {}
    for s in seeds: distinct[s] = true
    print("Consecutive identical seeds: %d / %d" % [ties, TRIALS - 1])
    print("Distinct seeds: %d / %d" % [distinct.size(), TRIALS])
    print("Elapsed: %.3f s   per-iter: %d ns" % [elapsed_us / 1e6, int(elapsed_us * 1000.0 / TRIALS)])
    get_tree().quit()
```

Results, Godot 4.6.2 stable headless release:

| Machine              | per-iter | Consecutive identical seeds | Distinct seeds (out of 1M) |
| -------------------- | -------: | --------------------------: | -------------------------: |
| M-series Mac         | 332 ns   | 669,907 / 999,999           | 330,093                    |
| Fast Windows desktop | 312 ns   | 688,573 / 999,999           | 311,427                    |

So roughly two-thirds of consecutive constructions get an identical seed value, and only about a third of all constructions across the run produced a distinct seed. Your earlier run with no overlap means your per-iteration time was over a microsecond on that machine, which is consistent with the 12,802 / 100M result we saw earlier; on faster setups the seeds collapse the way the formula predicts.

Will update the PR test to assert on `seed` directly instead of comparing `randi()` output, and fix the "1 to 5 us" wording.

> While I can confirm the specific scenario with a faster template I don't see that this is a remotely common use case, generating a large number of RNGs in a without some custom seeding mechanism seems very very niche and potentially a code smell, and I think it would be better to document that creating RNGs very rapidly can cause the seeds to overlap, and suggest using other means to improve this

Great you can reproduce. On the "very niche" framing, per-instance RNGs are actually the natural design in a few common patterns. Each card or die in a card-and-dice game can own its own RNG so a reroll is independent of whatever particles, AI tie-breaks, or SFX consumed randomness in the same frame. A chunked procgen world seeds a per-chunk RNG from `world_seed XOR chunk_id` so chunks can run in parallel and produce the same content regardless of order. A networked or replay-driven game derives each entity's stream from its identifier so two clients agree on outcomes without having to agree on global execution order. A loot system creates a fresh RNG per chest from `(chest_id, run_seed)` so chest A always gives the same drop regardless of which chests were opened first. All four are awkward boilerplate on top of a single shared RNG, and none of them is "constructing many RNGs at the same instant on purpose"; they're cases where independent per-owner streams happen to be created during normal gameplay flow.

On documenting versus fixing, my concern with the doc-only path is that the class reference already advertises independent per-instance state ("multiple instances, each with their own seed and state"). A footnote saying "actually do not rely on this if you create them quickly" doesn't repair the contract, it contradicts it. A small fix in the seeder lets the documented behavior just work, including for plugin authors and future users who never see the warning.

If the team's preference is genuinely "document instead", I'd at least suggest framing it as a known limitation marked for fixing later rather than as intended behavior, since the latter sets a contract the rest of the docs do not currently support. But if you plan on fixing it later, well, the PR already fixes it.

> Each card or die in a card-and-dice game can own its own RNG so a reroll is independent of whatever particles

Can you provide some example of this? Also they wouldn't have their RNGs initialized in a single loop like this would they? With no other initialization

> already advertises independent per-instance state

That isn't really what it says though, it makes no guarantee of uniqueness, and it says the seed is time based, so there's no broken contract here, just a lack of specificity

Sure, concrete cases where multiple `RandomNumberGenerator` instances do get constructed in close succession during normal gameplay:

- **Wave spawn**: an enemy wave spawns 20 to 50 mooks in a single frame. Each one constructs its own state (position, behavior tree, AI seed for variation). The construction loop in the spawn handler builds them back to back and the RNGs are part of `_init`.
- **Drawing a hand**: dealing 5 to 7 cards at start of turn, each card object constructs its RNG for per-card random effects. Five `Card.new()` calls happen in microseconds.
- **Save load**: a save with hundreds of game objects deserialises in a tight loop on load. Each object's `_init` runs, including any owned RNG.
- **Procgen feature pass**: world generation walks a list of chunk features (rooms, chests, NPC seeds, etc.) and instantiates each. Each feature's RNG is seeded from `(world_seed, feature_id)` if you use `set_seed`, but the user only learns to do that once they hit the bug; the natural code path is `RandomNumberGenerator.new()`.

You're right that none of these are "an empty loop initialising RNGs and nothing else", they always involve other init work. But the other work is typically lighter than the RNG construction itself (a few field assignments), so the inter-construction gap stays under a microsecond on modern hardware. That's enough to trigger the collision.

On the contract question, fair, the docs don't explicitly say "unique", and "time based seed" can be read narrowly. My read is that "multiple instances, each with their own seed and state" reads naturally as "different per instance" rather than "each instance has its own variable holding the same value as its predecessor". I'd be surprised if many users interpret the current text as a hint that consecutive instances might collide. Adding a "may collide if created within one microsecond" caveat would technically resolve the ambiguity, but it would also be a step the API surface itself doesn't currently signal, so users still won't expect it unless they read the warning.

I am of the opinion that this is an extremely niche use case

EDIT: and that a docs change specifying "collides if used within the same microsecond" would probably be enough

I also personally think that this is... so niche. I do agree with the reasons replied as to why.
"Randomness" and "uniqueness" are not the same thing, the docs do not seem to imply they're even the same thing, and in practical use-cases this quirk is either humanly imperceptible or is the result of questionable practices.

The issue *proves* that it's possible that a conflict can happen, but it doesn't make a clear argument as to what problem the conflict may cause.
In **all** of [the examples provided above](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/119322#issuecomment-4406036090), it would be more reasonable to use a **single** RandomNumberGenerator instance to fetch random numbers from. Instantiating multiple RandomNumberGenerator objects to generate numbers, and then freeing them, is both inefficient and impractical.
